title: The Worst Stocks in America

beats.text: The day war broke out in Europe, a young man ordered the worst stocks in America.
Every stock on the New York exchange under one dollar. A hundred shares of each.
Imagine you're his broker, reading that list.
A hundred and four companies. Thirty-four already bankrupt.
The buyer is John Templeton, a young Tennessean who paid for college with poker winnings.
And he's buying with borrowed money, while everyone else sells.
So why buy bankrupt companies in the middle of a war?
You see, an umbrella shop in a drought sells for pennies.
Nobody wants it. Then it rains.
The war was the rain. Idle factories filled with orders.
Within about four years, his junk pile was up roughly four hundred percent.
Only four of those companies ended up worthless.
He called it buying at the point of maximum pessimism.
And years later, his one regret?

facts.claim: In 1939, when World War II broke out in Europe (September 1939), Templeton had his broker buy (he said he called the day the war began)
100 shares each of every NYSE stock selling at $1 a share or less
104 companies, including 34 in bankruptcy (Wikipedia says 37; the Washington Post obituary, The Week/WSJ, Morningstar and Motley Fool say 34)
He bought with borrowed money (The Week/WSJ give $10,000; single source, left out of narration)
Born 1912 in Winchester, Tennessee; paid for Yale with poker winnings
US industry picked up because of the war, which made the purchases pay off
After an average holding period of about four years the portfolio returned about 400 percent
Only four of the companies turned out worthless
He described his method as buying at the point of maximum pessimism
He later said he wished he had held those stocks longer
The broker (the viewer) and the umbrella shop are illustrative, not historical

caption:
September 1939: as war broke out in Europe, a young John Templeton bought 100 shares of every NYSE stock under $1. 104 companies, 34 of them bankrupt.
Only four ended up worthless, and the pile returned about 400% in roughly four years.
